archetype.name: Pocket Passer (developing, intermediate-first)
archetype.definition: A second-year passer who wins from the pocket on short and 10-to-19-yard throws, gets the ball out faster than he did as a rookie, and uses his legs as a sound complement rather than a primary weapon.

report.headline: Cleaner, quicker year two, but the deep ball and third downs still sink him.
report.take:
Cam Ward's second season is a real but incomplete step forward. The rookie-year problems were accuracy and holding the ball, and both have moved. His completion rate is up 4.6 points, CPOE up 3.1, bad-throw rate down 4.7 points, and time to throw has dropped from 3.0 to 2.85 seconds. The clearest change is under pressure. He went from taking sacks on 32% of pressures last year (35th of 62) to 17.1% now, 4th of 45. He is processing faster and throwing it away or checking down instead of absorbing hits. The overall line is still below average: -0.06 EPA per dropback (34th of 55) and 6.19 yards per attempt (37th). The improvement shows up as fewer disasters, not more big plays.

The passing profile splits sharply by depth. In the 10-to-19-yard window he is good: +0.343 EPA per attempt, four touchdowns, and the largest positive chunk of value in his game. Two ends of the field drag that down. Behind the line, screens and swing passes have cost -14.7 EPA in total, and Tony Pollard's -0.344 EPA per target is the clearest symptom. Twenty-plus yards downfield, he has completed 17.9% with a -20.6 CPOE, no touchdowns and two picks. That is not a scheme quirk. He is simply not connecting deep. Add an air-yards-to-sticks figure of -2.28 and you get the third-down problem: a 27.8% conversion rate facing an average of 8.2 yards to go.

The last three games look like a breakout on paper: +0.018 EPA per dropback, 7.84 adjusted net yards per dropback, two touchdown passes a game. Context tempers it. Two of those games were shootouts against Cincinnati and Dallas, the league's worst defense by EPA now. He was trailing for long stretches against a Titans defense that ranks 31st against the pass and last in explosive passes allowed. His trailing-by-9-plus CPOE (+5.9) is far better than his one-score CPOE (-3.3). In the one top-tier test of that stretch, Jacksonville in Week 10, he completed 28 of 39 but posted -6.3 passing EPA on a 5.6-yard intended air depth. The credible encouragement is a +0.265 EPA per play in close fourth quarters, where trailing-script padding doesn't apply.

The rushing is a quiet plus: +0.375 EPA per carry, scrambles worth +0.341 each, and three rushing touchdowns. The fumbles are not. Two lost (43rd of 55) and four turnover-worthy fumbles are a ball-security issue worth flagging for a player whose sack avoidance has otherwise improved. The arc points toward a competent starter. Whether he becomes more than that depends on finding a deep ball, and nothing in this season says that is close.

strengths.title: Pressure handling transformed from year one
strengths.body: He converts pressure into sacks at one of the lowest rates in the league, a dramatic flip from his rookie season. Faster processing is behind it: time to throw is down and bad throws have fallen sharply. Because it lines up with a measurable change in how quickly he releases the ball, it looks like real development rather than luck, and should mostly hold.

strengths.title: Intermediate window is his money zone
strengths.body: Throws of 10-19 air yards produce +0.343 EPA per attempt and four of his ten touchdowns. This is where his anticipation shows and where Carnell Tate has become the most productive target on the team. It is a sustainable skill, and the offense would benefit from leaning into it on early downs.

strengths.title: Efficient, selective runner
strengths.body: He doesn't run much, but when he does it adds value, both on scrambles and on designed keepers near the goal line. That gives the offense a reliable bailout on broken plays and a short-yardage option. Low volume caps the fantasy impact, though the efficiency is real.

concerns.title: No functioning deep ball
concerns.body: On 28 throws of 20-plus air yards he has completed 17.9%, with a CPOE of -20.6, no touchdowns and two interceptions. A deep threat's catch rate is always low, but this is far below expected, not just low. He has also become less aggressive than last year. Until it improves, defenses can squeeze everything underneath, and that caps his yards per attempt.

concerns.title: Third downs and the short-of-sticks habit
concerns.body: He converts 27.8% of third downs, and those plays have cost -23 EPA, nearly all of his season deficit. Part of it is offense-wide: long average distances and a screen game that loses value. Part is him: his average throw lands well short of the sticks. That is the cost of the quicker, safer process, and it will persist until he trusts throws past the marker.

concerns.title: Recent surge leans on soft scripts
concerns.body: The last-three-game jump came with the Titans trailing in shootouts, including against the league's worst defense. He is more accurate when down two scores than in one-score games. Some of the improvement is real, but expect part of it to fade against better defenses.

trend.note: Weeks 1-7 were mostly negative-EPA games with rough bad-throw rates. Since Week 8 he has thrown two touchdowns in each game and posted positive EPA in two of three. The exception was the Jacksonville game, where the short game got smothered.

nextGame.headline: Rematch with a defense that already smothered his short game
nextGame.body:
Jacksonville is the worst stylistic matchup on his schedule. It ranks 1st against short passes and 1st against the run, which closes off the two things Tennessee does most willingly. In Week 10 he threw it short (5.6 intended air yards), completed 28 of 39, and still lost 6.3 EPA. The openings are real but narrow. The Jaguars are only 21st on deep passes and 30th in sack rate, and offenses throw against them well above normal. A two-touchdown spread in a 47.5 total also points to Tennessee trailing and throwing a lot. Volume should be there, but efficiency probably won't be unless he finally hits something downfield, which is exactly his weakest area.

On his side, left tackle Dan Moore Jr. (96% of snaps) is questionable with a knee injury. Moore was hurt in Dallas, the game where Ward took five sacks and held the ball 3.35 seconds. If Moore sits, the sack-avoidance gains get tested even against a weak pass rush. Tyjae Spears on IR removes a part-time back and funnels more backfield targets to Pollard, whose targets have been a drain. For Jacksonville, rotational edge rushers Matt Dickerson and Danny Striggow are out, thinning an already low-sack front. Corner Jarrian Jones (64% of snaps) is questionable. The Jaguars' center and a tackle are also hurt, which could slow their offense a little, but not enough to change the expected script.

keyMatchups.title: Short passes into the league's best
keyMatchups.body: Jacksonville allows the lowest EPA in the league on short throws, and that is where most of his attempts go. The first meeting showed it: a high completion rate but negative value. He must push the ball into the intermediate range to move the chains.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots against a softer back end
keyMatchups.body: The Jaguars are vulnerable deep, a rare weakness on an otherwise stingy unit. But his 20-plus accuracy is the worst part of his game, so it is a matchup he hasn't shown he can exploit. One or two connections would swing his day.

keyMatchups.title: Target funnel away from TE and backs
keyMatchups.body: Jacksonville has been the stingiest defense on tight end and lead-back targets, but generous to third receivers. That points his reads toward Elic Ayomanor and the outside wideouts rather than Gunnar Helm or Pollard checkdowns.

nextGame.watch: How often he attacks past 10 air yards early, rather than living underneath the way he did in the Week 10 loss.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is steadier than his rookie year: better accuracy, faster release, far fewer sacks per pressure, and a useful running game. A Titans defense this porous will keep producing trailing scripts and pass volume. That supports roughly 205 to 250 passing yards a game and steady fantasy floors even when efficiency is poor. The last-three-game touchdown rate is the piece most likely to regress, because it came partly in shootouts and against the league's worst defense. Something like 1.1 to 1.7 touchdown passes a game is a fairer expectation than two.

What would make this more than a competent-floor season is the deep ball and third downs. Neither has shown real signs of turning, and the screen game around him is a drag. Expect EPA per dropback to hover near league average at best (-0.05 to +0.02). The fumbles are a lower-probability but real risk to watch.
swingFactors: Dan Moore Jr.'s knee and left-tackle stability
How often a leaky defense forces trailing, pass-heavy scripts

confidence.note: Ten starts plus a full rookie year show clear trait changes, but the recent surge rests on three games with favorable scripts.
